extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science, journalism, communication, and public affairs; general readers interested in public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks and principles for understanding how public opinion is formed and functions — focusing on mental images, pseudo-environments, symbols, news, and the relation between belief and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular relationship: scene, picture, and response
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis must recognize the triangular relationship between the real scene of action, the human picture of that scene (the mental image), and the human response to that picture as it plays out on the scene of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann asserts the analyst of public opinion should begin by recognizing this triangle; he gives theatrical and cinematic metaphors (actors guided by an imagined play, a moving picture that fades into a reenactment of inner motive) and concrete political examples (Senate debate over a rumored landing of American marines) to show how the picture in men's heads explains exterior behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: People act on a pseudo-environment, not directly on reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavior is a response to a constructed 'pseudo-environment' — the representation of the world people carry in their minds — rather than to the objective environment itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Lippmann's central concept: examples include isolated islanders continuing false beliefs until a delayed newspaper arrives, a girl who interprets a broken window as news of a death, and large-scale political actions (nations at war believing in self-defense) driven by divergent pseudo-environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictions and schematic models are necessary tools (not merely lies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictions range from hallucination to scientists' schematic models; human thought depends on simplified representations of the overwhelmingly complex real environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann emphasizes that the alternative — direct acquaintance with the real environment — is impossible due to complexity; he notes that a fiction's value depends on its degree of fidelity and warns against mistaking the map for the territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps of the world (mental models) must be evaluated for bias from needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental maps are often sketched to serve personal or group needs; evaluators should check whether one's maps have been distorted by these needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase from the text: 'Their persistent difficulty is to secure maps on which their own need, or someone else's need, has not sketched in the coast of Bohemia.' Illustrations include explorers seeking fountains of youth or diggers treating fool's gold as real gold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic personalities (heroes and devils) organize public feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Populations often concentrate feeling on symbolic personalities who stand for broader hopes or fears; these symbolic pictures can grant near-omnipotence to heroes and devils in public imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann documents hero-worship (the mass adoration of General Joffre) and the symmetric creation of 'devils' (e.g., blaming the Kaiser or Lenin for all evil) as mechanisms by which complex events are reduced to simple personified explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: In times of moderate security, symbols are checked by competing pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: When society is not wholly dominated by fear or passion, symbolic pictures are more numerous, smaller in scope, and subject to verification, comparison, and argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the armistice Lippmann shows how the large symbolic pictures (Allied Unity, national crusades) fragmented quickly as party, class, and personal interests reasserted themselves; normal times invite conflict, choice, and compromise that check single dominant symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: To understand actions, know what others believe they know
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding another's acts requires knowing the picture they have in their head; actions toward events one has not experienced are guided by the mental image of that event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the mining-town girl's grief over a broken pane (interpreted through local superstition) and by politicians acting on misreported facts; Lippmann argues that knowing others' beliefs is prerequisite to interpreting their behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda functions by altering the pictures to which people respond
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda aims to substitute one social pattern or picture for another so as to change behavior; class consciousness and national consciousness are cited as examples of such manufactured pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann points out that Marxian communists place hope in forming class-conscious groups through propaganda; more generally, efforts to shape public opinion work by changing the mental maps people use to predict outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan needs can produce credulity and rapid acceptance of rumors
rubrics_metrics.description: Partisanship and emotional investment predispose actors (including trained professionals) to accept and act upon unverified reports that fit their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Senate example: Senators treated a rumor (marines landed by foreign authority) as fact because it served partisan aims against the League of Nations; Lippmann uses this to warn how emotion and need can override evidentiary caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different private pseudo-environments complicate social coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Because individuals and groups possess varied and often incompatible pictures of the world, expecting identical behavior across diverse mental environments is unrealistic; social order is often founded on coincidence rather than shared understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann quotes Chesterton's lamp-post metaphor and enumerates the many centers of authority and association (governments, parties, corporations, clubs) to show how variety in private beliefs undermines simple unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public persona vs private self must be distinguished in interpreting leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men and public figures commonly have constructed public personas distinct from their private selves; biographies and public portrayals often capture different 'selves' and should be read accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the contrast between official biographies (public life) and revealing memoirs (private life), the staged presence of maps on a general's office wall for photographs, and the observation that even valets may inhabit the fiction of their masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions based on pseudo-environments have consequences in the real environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Although stimulated by false or simplified pictures, behaviors still occur in, and produce effects in, the real world; mismatch between picture and reality leads to maladjustment and costly errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann warns of the practical costs of acting on fictions — 'butting one's head against a stone wall' and Herbert Spencer's image of a 'Beautiful Theory' killed by a 'Gang of Brutal Facts' — stressing the need to account for real-world consequences when evaluating beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysts should avoid generalizing about innate human nature without controlling for differences in environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about what people 'are' or how they necessarily behave are unreliable unless one accounts for the widely differing pseudo-environments that shape responses; environment and constructed pictures jointly determine behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann treats the pseudo-environment as a hybrid of nature and conditions and uses it to critique hasty inferences in nature-vs-nurture debates: different observed behaviors may reflect distinct pictures rather than immutable human traits.
